newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Burning fields see Tajik peace up in smoke.
newsitem.headline: Burning fields see Tajik peace up in smoke.

text.p: Burning fields saw Tajikistan's hard won peace go up in smoke on Tuesday as government forces in the former Soviet republic rocketed positions held by a mutinous colonel south of the capital.

Clouds of acrid brown smoke hung over the Fakhrobad valley as the presidential guard, loyal to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, unleashed clutches of Grad rockets against troops fighting for renegade Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev.

"Khudoyberdyev still controls Fakhrobad and commands the heights," said a pro-government commander. He said his forces had started the rocket strikes at about 3.30 pm (1030 GMT) in the valley 25 km (15 miles) south of Dushanbe.
There have been no reliable casualty figures, although the International Red Cross said at the weekend it had provided medicine for 40 wounded in Dushanbe.

The eruption of fighting on Saturday is not linked to the republic's armed Islamic opposition, with whom the government signed a peace accord in June aimed at ending four years of civil war. That conflict claimed tens of thousands of lives.
The latest clashes show Rakhmonov's grip on power as tenuous as ever and the impoverished republic far from the peace craved by its 5.7 million population.

"Where can we run to?" said 17-year-old Nargis near Kirov, 18 km (12 miles) south of Dushanbe. Her red dress printed with roses vivid against the brown, smoke-covered hills behind her, Nargis said: "There's war everywhere else too".
A group of men in the village sat on their haunches and chewed over the situation next to a burbling irrigation ditch.
"We can't bring the harvest in," said Andrakhmad Yurov, 38 and a smallholder. "We're all sitting here waiting for a lull".

Conversation was brought to an abrupt halt by several loud cracks as presidential guards nearby fired a salvo of Grad rockets -- fast, bright needles leaving trails of smoke -- over their heads and into the valley.
"If the government is not strong enough, it means more civil war," sighed Yurov.
Khudoyberdyev, 34, the commander of an elite government armoured brigade, has mutinied twice before in as many years.
He moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend in the wake of fighting between two rival warlords in the capital.
The renegade colonel has not revealed his motives but he is counted by western diplomats as a potential coup maker.

"I'm not trying to move on Dushanbe," Khudoyberdyev told Reuters by telephone earlier on Tuesday. "Government forces provoked us by moving toward Kurgan Tyube (his headquarters) -- we had to defend ourselves".
On Sunday, Rakhmonov issued a three-day ultimatum to Khudoyberdyev to lay down his arms or face "destruction".
Gun law has seen Tajikistan divided up into a complicated patchwork of independent fiefdoms under the control of armed groups like those in neighbouring Afghanistan.
Khudoyberdyev said aircraft had bombed Kalininabad, a town near his base about 120 km (80 miles) south of Dushanbe.
He lost control of a strategically important aluminium smelter west of the capital to the presidential guard on Monday.
Russia, which deploys 20,000 troops in the Central Asian state and which fears unrest along its unstable southern rim, has been cautious in its reaction to the fighting.
On Tuesday, the predominantly Russian peacekeeping force in Tajikistan fielded by the Commonwealth of Independent States said it would stay neutral and take no part in the conflict.
